title: The Clinical Spectrum and Neurodevelopmental Pathogenesis of KPTN ‐Related Disorder in a Mouse Model

sections.abstract:
Pathogenic variants in Kaptin (KPTN) cause KPTN‐related disorder (KRD). KPTN modulates mTOR signaling activation within the KICSTOR complex in response to cellular amino acid levels. We define the clinical spectrum and investigate the developmental pathogenesis of KRD.

We report the genotype and clinical phenotype of 71 KRD individuals (28 female subjects, ages 1 to 55 years) including 48 newly identified KRD individuals. The effects of Kptn knockout on brain development were assayed in vitro and in vivo.

We defined 15 novel KPTN variants. Intellectual disability (ID) was identified in all KRD individuals. Macrocephaly and epilepsy were observed in 46% and 47%, respectively. Neuroimaging revealed megalencephaly but no overt structural abnormalities. Ketotic hypoglycemia and endocrinopathies were identified in KRD. Increased head size was detected in unaffected parents heterozygous for KPTN variants. Two KRD individuals with drug‐resistant epilepsy were treated with the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus but did not exhibit improved seizure control. CRISPR/Cas9 Kptn knockout in vitro induced mTOR activation and an mTOR‐dependent increase in cell size. Kptn−/− mice exhibited increased cortical mTOR signaling that was reduced by rapamycin. Heterotopic neurons were identified in the subcortical white matter in the Kptn −/− mouse. Focal CRISPR/Cas9 Kptn knockout in cortex via in utero electroporation resulted in white matter heterotopic neurons. Electroencephalogram (EEG) did not detect ictal or inter‐ictal abnormalities.

KRD is a multisystem neurodevelopmental disorder associated with ID, macrocephaly, epilepsy, mTOR signaling hyperactivation, and in a mouse model, subtle structural alterations in cerebral cortical cytoarchitecture. ANN NEUROL 2026;99:1287–1302
sections.methods:
The clinical cohort is an observational study including male and female individuals with a confirmed molecular diagnosis of KRD. Male and female mice were experimentally examined.

Differences in cell size, cell proliferation, and immunofluorescence were determined using 1‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) between groups ( p < 0.05 to p < 0.001). Quantification of normalized fluorescence intensity data (arbitrary units [Aus]) was performed in Origin statistical software using ANOVA ( p < 0.05). Experimenters were blinded to condition and treatment during all experimental analysis. Sample size for animal studies was based on power analysis. No outliers or other data were excluded in either clinical or experimental analysis.

Experiments were approved by the University of Maryland School of Medicine Institutional Animal Care and Use (IACUC) Committees (Protocol #0822001). Clinical research was performed with informed consent from the affected individual or their legal guardian. Institutional study approvals include Akron Children's Hospital (institutional review board [IRB] 986876‐3) and University of Arizona (IRB 10‐0050‐010). The parents of 2 affected individuals gave and signed consent for the sirolimus trial treatment under compassionate use indication for severe DRE. Informed consent for publication of facial images (Fig 2 ) was provided by all patients or their legal guardians.

Craniofacial features of children and adults with KRD. Note subtle facial dysmorphism. Facial appearance of 24 newly identified individuals with KRD, identifiable features include frontal bossing, a prominent chin, small downslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, a broad nasal tip, thick vermillion of the lower lip, and mild retrognathia. KRD = KPTN ‐related disorder. [Color figure can be viewed at www.annalsofneurology.org ]

Individuals with KRD were identified by their clinician, GeneMatcher, the Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) project (Complementary Analysis Project [CAP] #255), the 100,000 genomes project, NHS Genomic Medicine Service, and our collaborative research network. Previously published cases were ascertained through a literature review. We adhered to the relevant STROBE checklist ( https://www.strobe-statement.org/checklists/ ).

Genomic studies (exome/genome sequencing or targeted variant analyses) to identify the genetic cause of KRD were performed as part of clinical and/or research investigations dependent on phenotypic presentation and family history in affected individuals and family members. Single‐nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotyping to assess mutational age of the Amish founder variants (c.776C>A p.Ser259* and c.714_731dup p.Met241_Gln246dup), was performed using Illumina HumanCytoSNP‐12 version 2.1 beadchip array.

Phenotypic information was obtained by the clinical care provider using a targeted questionnaire (Supplementary Table S1 ). All OFC z‐scores were recalculated using measurements and known age at assessment (gestation‐adjusted where needed) using the British 1990 growth reference 15 to ensure all values were comparable. Affected individuals were examined by providers according to routine clinical standards relevant to their clinical presentation.

A single guide RNA (gRNA) targeting exon 6 of Kptn was generated in silico using ChopChop software ( chopchop.cbu.uib.no ; Fig 3 ; see Supplementary Data S 3 ). A scramble gRNA sequence was used as a transfection and gRNA control. The gRNAs were inserted into Cas9 and RFP containing plasmids (PX458; Addgene #48138) using Golden Gate Assembly. Neuro2a cells (N2aC; Sigma‐Aldrich) were used to define the consequences of CRISPR/Cas9 mediated Kptn KO versus scramble control and wildtype (WT) cells. N2a cells were lipid transfected with plasmids using Lipofectamine LTX with Plus reagent (ThermoFisher Scientific) for 48 hours. Transfected cells were FAC sorted based on RFP fluorescence at the University of Maryland School of Medicine Flow Cytometry Core, re‐plated, and grown to confluence.

Kptn KO in vitro via CRISPR/Cas9 causes mTOR activation. (A) Guide RNA (gRNA) sequence targeting Kptn exon 6 in red. (B) RT‐PCR showing reduced Kptn mRNA in Kptn KO versus scrambled (scram) gRNA transfected cells (*** p < 0.001). (C) Western blot assay showing absent Kptn and increased S6 protein phosphorylation in N2a cells after Kptn KO. β‐Actin is used as a protein loading control. (D) Western blot assays showing reduced S6 phosphorylation in WT, scramble, and Kptn KO cells following rapamycin (left) or torin1 (middle) treatment or amino acid free conditions (right) in Kptn KO cells. Graphs show average normalized levels of phosphorylated S6 (PS6) relative to S6 and β‐Actin protein expression (** p < 0.05, *** p < 0.001). AAF = amino acid free media; KO = knockout; RT‐PCR = reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction; UT = untreated; WT = wildtype. [Color figure can be viewed at www.annalsofneurology.org ]

A loss‐of‐function mouse KRD model was generated at Wellcome Sanger Institute's Mouse Genetics Project (see Supplementary Data S 3 ). 14

See Supplementary Data S 3 . 16

Kptn expression and changes in mTOR signaling were defined by Western blot assay in lysates from human HEK293T and SY5Y cells, in murine N2a cell lines (Supplementary Fig S5 ), and in tissue homogenates from Kptn−/− mouse brains. To define the mTOR‐dependency of cell signaling changes, cells were treated with rapamycin, torin1 (a highly selective mTORC1 and mTORC2 kinase inhibitor), vehicle (DMSO), or incubated in amino acid‐free cell culture media for 60 minutes each.

Single cell digital images were captured at 20× magnification and analyzed in Imaris software for total pixels of the soma area and converted to μm 2 in Excel (Microsoft, Redmond, WA). Soma diameter was measured across the longest dimension of each soma (25 cells in each of 2 biological replicates). To define the mTOR‐dependency of cell size changes, cells were incubated for 24 hours in complete media with the mTOR inhibitors rapamycin or torin1 (each 50 nM; DMSO was vehicle control); because of the longer incubation time, lower doses of each were used to avoid cell death.

See Supplementary Data S 3 .

Electroencephalogram (EEG) electrodes were implanted into Kptn −/− mice at P35 and secured onto the skull 3 mm behind bregma under isoflurane anesthesia. Continuous video‐EEG recordings (5 days) were performed using Pinnacle Technology 3 channel EEG system (Lawrence, KS). Video‐EEGs were reviewed manually without knowledge of mouse genotype to assess electrographic and behavioral abnormalities consistent with seizures including interictal epileptiform discharges and spontaneous seizures. Another group of mice received the pro‐convulsant agent pentylenetetrazol (PTZ; 55 mg/kg i.p.) and recorded for 30 minutes to capture the time to first electrographic seizure detected by EEG (latency to seizure onset). Thirty minutes after PTZ injection, the experiment was terminated, and the animals were euthanized using CO 2 asphyxiation and cervical dislocation. EEG power spectra were extracted using Seizure Pro software (Pinnacle Technology, Lawrence, KS). Total power, gamma, alpha, beta, delta, and theta bands were acquired at 10‐second intervals across an approximately 72‐hour continuous EEG. The EEG traces were examined visually for significant artifacts, and EEGs channels resulting in anomalous power data were excluded from the analysis, defined as EEGs with high amplitude movement artifacts or low amplitude signals. Each spectral band across each genotype was averaged and graphed in GraphPad Prism 10. Data were analyzed using a 1‐way ANOVA with a p < 0.05 deemed significant.
sections.results:
We investigated the clinical phenotype and genotype of 71 affected individuals (28 female subjects and 43 male subjects, aged = 1.5 to 55 years) with a confirmed molecular diagnosis of KRD (Tables 1A and 1B ). This included 7 newly identified KRD individuals (individuals 1–5, 9, and 10) with Anabaptist (Amish/Mennonite) heritage and 41 with no known Anabaptist heritage (see Table 1A , Supplementary Table S2 , Supplementary Data S 1 , and Supplementary Fig S1 ). We also revisited 9 Ohio Anabaptist individuals with KRD originally described by our group 2 including 3 deceased brothers (individuals A–C, from accidental death, head injury, and pneumonia, respectively), and reviewed available clinical data for 14 individuals in 7 previously published studies 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 (Supplementary Table S3 ). We excluded 2 siblings (affected individuals X and Y; see Supplementary Table S3 ) previously published due to discrepancy in phenotypic features, alternative genetic diagnosis (pathogenic SON variant), and uncertain significance of the identified KPTN missense variant.

Summary of the Clinical Features of 71 Individuals With KRD

Clinical features observed in 71 individuals with KRD, listed as a percentage of individuals with a characteristic and the number of individuals shown as a fraction in brackets. Patients are further divided into 3 subgroups by type of variant at each KPTN allele: biallelic predicted LoF variants (nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice variant), biallelic protein altering variants (missense, small indels) or compound heterozygous for one LoF and one protein altering variant.

LoF, loss of function; M, male; F, female; SD, standard deviation.

Summary of the clinical and behavioral features of 71 individuals with KRD

Clinical features observed in 71 individuals with KRD, listed as a percentage of individuals with a characteristic and the number of individuals shown as a fraction in brackets. Patients are further divided into 3 subgroups by type of variant at each KPTN allele: biallelic predicted LoF variants (nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice variant), biallelic protein altering variants (missense, small indels) or compound heterozygous for one LoF and one protein altering variant.

LoF, loss of function; M, male; F, female; SD, standard deviation.

We previously reported 14 OFC data for 20 individuals with KRD and data from an additional 22 newly identified individuals are presented here. In 95% (40/42) individuals, OFC was above the mean, varying between +0.14 and +6.11 SDs. Only 36% (15/42) of individuals were macrocephalic (defined as ≥2 SDs above the mean) with the average OFC +2.08 SDs. Previous reports suggested that ME was an almost invariable feature of KRD, with 78% 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 displaying ME at diagnosis (average OFC +2.8 SD). Overall, ME was observed in 48% (29/60) of all reported individuals with KRD. Possible explanations for this difference include ascertainment bias given that ME was previously considered a cardinal feature of KRD, expansion of the phenotypic spectrum, and the progressive nature of the ME (see below).

Birth OFC measurements were available for 25 of 71 individuals, 44% (11/25) had an OFC below the mean and only individuals 7 and 28 were macrocephalic at birth. The combined OFC Z‐score measurements for 59 individuals with KRD demonstrates a rapid increase in OFC within the first 6 months of life (Fig 1B ). This finding is further illustrated with example measurements from an affected male subject (individual 32; Supplementary Fig S2 ) and affected female subject (individual 14; see Supplementary Fig S2 ). In summary, OFC measurements are within the normal range at birth in the majority of KRD affected individuals, with ME developing within the first 6 months, demonstrating postnatal progressive ME.

Neuroimaging in 46 of 71 individuals with KRD (36 brain magnetic resonance imaging [MRI] scans, 10 computed tomography [CT] scans, and 1 ultrasound [US]; see Table 1A , Supplementary Tables S2 and S3 , and Supplementary Fig S3 ), identified generalized ME in 22 individuals with no overt structural abnormalities (see Supplementary Fig S3A–F ). Other recurrent findings included mild ventriculomegaly (8/46), pineal cyst (3/46), cavum septum pellucidum (2/46), and flattened pituitary gland (2/46).

Intellectual disability (assessed using Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition [DSM‐5] criteria) is a universal feature described in all individuals with KRD and varies from mild to profound (see Table 1A , and Supplementary Tables S2 and S3 ). Although no genotype–phenotype correlation could be identified, severity of intellectual disability appears to increase with age and the presence of and poor control of seizures. Developmental delay is a variable feature, observed in 94% (67/71) with 9 non‐verbal individuals. Detailed psychometric testing previously published by our group compared 6 Amish individuals with KRD (individuals C‐G and I) and age‐matched Amish controls, 11 and identified a moderate level of ID (mean Full Scale Intelligence Quotient [FSIQ] of 43; Z‐score = 3.83) with significant impairment in all cognitive domains except narrative memory (see Supplementary Tables S2 and S3 ) in KRD.

Seizures were confirmed in 47% (33/70) of individuals with KRD, with variable age of onset between neonatal period and 32 years (see Table 1A and Supplementary Table S4 ). Nine individuals had DRE despite polytherapy including a single individual previously reported who died at the age of 9 from status epilepticus (individual L). 6 In 33% (11/33) of the individuals with epilepsy, seizures resolved with advancing age. To date, no particular anti‐seizure medication appears to be more effective for seizure control in KRD. EEGs available for 8 affected individuals (4, 7, 14–17, 33, and 48) showed generalized slowing, multifocal epileptiform discharges, and frequent focal sharp wave activity.

Behavioral features are a common (85%; 55/65 individuals) but variable feature in KRD including anxiety, panic attacks, stereotypies (hand flapping/clapping/rubbing, head banging, and rocking), tics, repetitive speech, hyperactivity, impaired social interactions, sleep disturbance, and increased tolerance to painful stimuli (see Tables 1B S2 and S3 ).

Craniofacial features are subtle (Fig 2 and see Tables 1B , S2 , and S3 ) and include frontal bossing, a prominent chin, small down slanting palpebral fissures, and hypertelorism (Supplementary Data S 1 ). The facial features of KRD become more prominent with advancing age. More variable clinical features observed in individuals with KRD (Supplementary Data S 1 ) include recurrent infections in 27% (16/60), skeletal abnormalities in 20% (12/59), ophthalmic features, and endocrine abnormalities. Importantly, we report 3 additional individuals with ketotic hypoglycemia, affecting 7% (4/58) of the KRD cohort.

We performed a systematic analysis of OFC in 42 heterozygous parents of identified KRD cases (see Supplementary Tables S2 and S3 ) and observed a significant increase in OFC size (mean Z‐score = 0.78, p = 0.01621) in carriers compared to the general population distribution, although infrequently in the macrocephalic range (7 out of 42 had an OFC >2 SDs; Fig 1C ). This confirms our previous observation that whereas KRD is an autosomal recessive condition, pathogenic KPTN alleles may exert a heterozygous effect on head size. 14 Although not systematically recorded, psychiatric illness has been reported in 4 heterozygous individuals from 3 nuclear families in our study, including severe depression (one incidence of suicide), anxiety, and obsessive‐compulsive disorder (OCD).

There are 22 identified pathogenic KPTN variants associated with KRD to date (Fig 1D , see Tables 2A , 2B ). Of the 48 affected individuals comprehensively phenotyped as part of this study, 34 (5 Amish/Mennonite and 29 individuals not known to have any Anabaptist heritage) were identified to have segregation of at least one of the 2 previously described Amish KPTN founder variants ( NM_007059.4 :Chr19:g.47479874G>T,c.776C>A p.Ser259* or Chr19:g.47479918G>GACCGACCACATCTGCAGA, c.714_731dup p.Met241_Gln246dup [hg38]; see Supplementary Tables S2 and S3 ). All variants were assessed to be pathogenic/likely pathogenic (ACMG/ACGS criteria, see Tables 2A , 2B ). Assessing the distribution of variants within the KPTN gene in relation to the protein domain architecture (see Fig 1D ), all 5 likely pathogenic KPTN missense variants are located within highly conserved residues of the integrin alpha domain and are predicted to be deleterious by in silico pathogenicity prediction tools and protein modeling studies (Fig 1D, E , Supplementary Fig S3G , and Supplementary Table S5 ). Additional genetic variants leading to concurrent diagnoses that could not be excluded as potentially contributing to the phenotype in 3 individuals (Supplementary Data S 1 ).

Newly Identified Pathogenic or Likely Pathogenic KPTN Variants Identified in Individuals With KRD

Genome wide SNP genotyping studies identifying the ancestral origin of the p.Ser259* and p.Met241_Gln246dup variants estimate these likely arose 18.5 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 11.1–25.8; approximately 220–520 years) and 34.4 (95% CI = 22.6–52.6; approximately 460–1060 years) generations ago, respectively (Supplementary Data S 2 and Supplementary Fig S4 ).

Based on our clinical data in this expanded phenotypic analysis, we propose clinical management guidelines for evaluation and care of patients with KRD (Supplementary Table S6 ) that include screening, surveillance, clinical evaluation, and treatment approaches.

Our current (see below) and published 14 preclinical data demonstrate a key role for KPTN in modulation of mTOR activity in the brain with clear evidence in vitro and in vivo that loss of KPTN leads to enhanced mTOR signaling. As with other mTORopathies, for example, tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), we hypothesized that overactive mTOR signaling may contribute to seizures in KRD . Previous clinical trials have demonstrated a limited benefit for mTOR inhibitors (mTORis) in DRE in TSC 17 and Pretzel syndrome, 18 both linked to hyperactivated mTOR pathway signaling. Thus, with consent from the parents, 2 individuals with KRD were treated with sirolimus for DRE in an expanded use paradigm. A 14‐year‐old girl (individual 14) with intellectual disability and drug‐resistant generalized tonic–clonic (GTC) seizures and focal impaired aware seizures (see Supplementary Tables S2 and S4 ) was trialed with sirolimus therapy (2–3 mg/day) as an adjunct to her regular medications (sodium valproate 375 mg t.i.d., zonisamide 150 mg b.i.d., and clonazepam prn) over a 6‐month period (4 months at 2 mg/day and 2 months at 3 mg/day). Despite adequate serum sirolimus levels, no significant change in seizure frequency was noted by her parents, who reported increased focal impaired aware seizures, often preceded by giggling (a new clinical semiology). Side effects reported included acne, diarrhea, fatigue, and increased serum cholesterol levels. The treatment trial was stopped after 6 months and seizure frequency and hyperlipidemia returned to baseline. A 16‐year‐old girl (individual 48) had persistent nocturnal GTC and myoclonic seizures resistant to multiple anti‐seizure medications (see Supplementary Tables S2 and S4 ). Regular medication eslicarbazepine (400 mg q.d.) was tapered and stopped, the sulthiame dose was reduced and sirolimus was added at 2 mg/day over a 3 to 4 week period. There were increased numbers of nocturnal and daytime seizures and thus, sirolimus was stopped.

KPTN protein was expressed in HEK293T, SY5Y cells, and N2A cell lines (see Supplementary Fig S5 ) and in tissue homogenates from mouse brains. KPTN is expressed in neurons in all cortical layers in WT mice and human cortex corroborating findings in the Allen Brain Atlas (see Supplementary Fig S5 ). 19

Sequencing showed Kptn sequence misalignment in the CRISPR‐edited KO N2a cell lines. In CRISPR‐edited KO N2a cells, reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT‐qPCR) showed reduced Kptn mRNA expression and Western blot assay showed a loss of Kptn protein expression (see Fig 3B, C ). Increased PS6 phosphorylation was observed in Kptn KO N2a cells versus control cells (scramble gRNA and WT) under complete media conditions (see Fig 3C ). PS6 levels returned to control cell levels following treatment with mTORis rapamycin (150 nM) or torin1 (100 nM). Persistent PS6 levels were seen in amino acid free conditions (see Fig 3D ) demonstrating that Kptn KO uncouples KICSTOR from mTOR inhibition even in the setting of nutrition deprivation.

Kptn KO N2a cell soma diameter was increased by 2‐fold (Fig 4 ; p < 0.05). Treatment with rapamycin (50 nM) or torin‐1 (50 nM) for 24 hours independently rescued cell soma enlargement in Kptn KO cells demonstrating that enhanced cell size was mTOR‐dependent. Previous work in the Kptn−/− mouse strain showed an increase in cellularity in layers II to V, 14 however EdU incorporation in vitro did not reveal evidence of enhanced cell proliferation following Kptn KO (Supplementary Fig S6 ). Using annexin V labeling, we found no change in cell death in Kptn KO N2a cells (see Supplementary Fig S6 ).

Kptn KO causes mTOR‐dependent increase in cell size. (A) Photomicrographs depicting N2a cell soma sizes in Kptn KO, scramble (scram) and WT cells. Cell soma diameter demonstrates a significant increase in mean cell area within Kptn KO cells compared with scramble control and WT N2a cell lines. (B) Quantification of relative changes in cell soma size in each condition ( red = Kptn−/− ; blue = Kptn+/− ; and green = WT mice; *** p < 0.0001). The increase in cell size was rescued following rapamycin or torin1 treatment. CMP = complete media only; KO = knockout; Veh = DMSO vehicle control; Rapa = rapamycin; WT = wildtype. [Color figure can be viewed at www.annalsofneurology.org ]

Previously, we showed a 7.9 to 14.4% increase in total brain area and an increase in cortical laminar area in Kptn −/− mice at 16 weeks post‐natal (P) age. 14 At P3 and P10, Kptn−/− and Kptn+/− brains were probed with NeuN antibodies to measure neuronal density and CTIP2 and SATB2 antibodies to define cortical laminar integrity. Supporting previous findings at P21, 14 neuronal density (number of NeuN‐labeled neurons per square millimeter of cortex) did not differ between Kptn−/− and Kptn+/− brains at P3 and P10 (not shown). CTIP2 immunolabeling in Kptn−/− mice was appropriately confined to layer V of the neocortex and SATB2 to layers II to IV and did not differ from Kptn+/− or WT mice (Supplementary Fig S7 ).

Quantification of NeuN labeling in 2 ROIs within the subcortical white matter beneath the frontal lobes and the somatosensory cortex revealed heterotopic neurons in the subcortical white matter in the Kptn−/− mouse compared with WT and heterozygous mice (Fig 5 ). To further assess the effects of Kptn KO on neuronal migration, we created focal Kptn KO during embryonic brain development using a CRISPR/Cas9 gRNA‐plasmid targeting Kptn delivered via in utero electroporation on E14. Postnatal days 1 to 3 (P1–3) pups were selected for histological analysis. Similar to the Kptn−/− mouse, Kptn KO neurons were observed within the subcortical white matter (Supplementary Fig S1 ; 6 animals per group, 3 sections per animal) and a small group of neurons were identified with birthdate inappropriate location in cortical layers IV to VI. When transfected with a scramble control plasmid, all neurons were observed appropriately in layer II/III with none observed in deeper layers or subcortical white matter. Thus, Kptn KO (either germline or focal) alters migration of a subset of neurons during cortical development.

Heterotopic neurons in pre‐frontal sub‐cortical white matter ROI. Rare NeuN‐labeled neurons seen sub‐cortical white matter (*) in WT and Kptn+/− (Het) mice (upper bracket demarcates cortex, lower bracket demarcates striatum, 10× magnification, scale bar = 500 μm). Right, and inset, multiple NeuN labeled heterotopic neurons seen in white matter ( arrows ) in Kptn−/− mice. Graph (bottom right) depicts increase in white matter neurons per defined ROI in Kptn−/− mice (KO) compared with WT and Kptn+/− (Het) mice (** p < 0.05). Het = heterozygous; KO = knockout; ROI = region of interest; WT = wildtype. [Color figure can be viewed at www.annalsofneurology.org ]

Phosphorylated S6 protein is enriched in layers III and V in WT and Kptn+/− cortex at P30. In contrast, Kptn−/− brains at P30 showed increased PS6 protein levels across cortical layers II to VI and dentate gyrus with no difference in unphosphorylated S6 expression demonstrating that Kptn loss leads to mTOR pathway activation (Fig 6 ). Importantly, treatment of mice with rapamycin once daily for 5 days from P30 to P35 reduced S6 phosphorylation across the cortex, hippocampal subfields, and dentate gyrus (see Fig 6 ).

The mTOR‐dependent changes in S6 phosphorylation in Kptn−/− mice. Left, in heterozygous and WT mice, S6 and PS6 are observed predominately in layers III and V at P30. In the Kptn−/− mice, elevated PS6 (Ser240/244) levels were observed ( star ) across all layers and the dentate gyrus ( arrow ). Daily rapamycin for 5 days (i.p. 5 mg/kg, P30–P35) resulted in a significant reduction of PS6 levels within the cortex, hippocampal subfields, and dentate gyrus in all genotypes. Graph (right) shows the average number of PS6‐labeled cells across groups (* p < 0.05; KO = red ; Het = blue ; and WT = grey ) and the reduction in PS6 labeled cells following rapamycin. Het = heterozygous; KO = knockout; WT = wildtype. [Color figure can be viewed at www.annalsofneurology.org ]

Continuous EEG was recorded for 5 days in mice at 5 weeks of age (P35). There were no clinical or behavioral events observed as seizures in the Kptn−/− , +/− , or WT control mice. Complete spectral analysis of Kptn−/− , +/− , and WT control mice did not reveal difference in EEG signatures in dark versus light conditions. Average power data for total, alpha, beta, gamma, delta, and theta bands did not reveal statistically significant differences between genotypes across any spectral band (Supplementary Fig S9 ). EEG recordings did not detect electrographic seizures and there were no inter‐ictal epileptiform discharges detected. Mice at P35 were treated with PTZ (55 mg/kg i.p.) and recorded for 40 minutes to capture the time to the first electrographic seizure. Kptn−/− mice did not demonstrate a reduced threshold for electrographic seizure onset following PTZ compared with Kptn +/− or WT mice (Supplementary Fig S10 ).
sections.discussion:
We report the genetic spectrum and clinical phenotype of 71 individuals with KRD including 38 previously unpublished individuals from 23 distinct geographical regions (14 from the Anabaptist community) and describe new features of KRD. Mild to profound ID is a universal feature of KRD, whereas ME and seizures are variable phenotypes in KRD. Kptn KO in vitro and in vivo led to enhanced mTOR signaling that was reduced by rapamycin treatment. The Kptn−/− mouse exhibits heterotopic neurons in the subcortical white matter and focal Kptn KO during embryonic brain development led to impaired cortical lamination. Clinical seizures and a reduced seizure threshold were not observed in Kptn−/− mice in keeping with the observation that more than half of KRD individuals do not have seizures. Sirolimus treatment of 2 KRD individuals did not affect seizure frequency.

Two distinct LoF founder variants in KPTN were initially reported in KRD, with affected individuals either homozygous or compound heterozygous for each variant. Subsequent studies have reported 14 individuals with phenotypic features overlapping those identified in the Amish population 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 20 and identifying 6 pathogenic KPTN variants including c.714_731dup p.Met241_Gln246dup originally identified in the Amish. In our cohort, 24 new individuals (individuals 11–34) inherited at least one copy of the p.Met241_Gln246dup variant allele, with 12 individuals (individuals 14–25) being homozygous for this variant. This is not an unexpected finding, as gnomAD v2.1.1/v4.10 estimates the overall carrier frequency of this variant as approximately 1 in 815 (Supplementary Fig S11 ), suggesting a live birth rate for homozygotes of approximately 1 in 2.7 million. Our haplotype data confirms this variant represents an ancestral founder mutation arising approximately 34.4 generations previously (see Supplementary Data S 2 and Supplementary Fig S4 ) in Europe prior to the migration of the Amish to the United States in the 17th to 18th centuries. The p.Ser259* variant was identified in a further 13 individuals and is estimated to have arisen more recently (approximately 18.5 generations ago). Both variants are present at low frequency in European populations but are present at significantly higher allele frequency in the Amish community, likely being introduced by early founders of the population. Five individuals (4 previously published) from 4 separate regions globally were found to display homozygous inheritance of the p.(Ser200Ilefs*55) variant, suggesting this represents another founder variant or recurrent mutation hotspot. We identify a further 15 KPTN variants in individuals with KRD (see Table 2A , 2B ), all with low frequencies in gnomAD and each classified as “likely pathogenic” or “pathogenic” according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG)/ Association for Clinical Genomic Science (ACGS) criteria.

In our cohort, 48% of individuals displayed ME at the time of assessment, although most had an OFC larger than average within +2 SDs of the mean. A diagnosis of KRD should not be excluded in individuals of normal head size, especially in infants, as ME develops postnatally in KRD. All but 2 individuals with KRD, had a normal head size at birth with a dramatic increase in OFC occurring within the 6 months of life and progressing into adulthood (eg, see Fig 1B and Supplementary Fig S2 ). Postnatal onset of ME may provide an early therapeutic window to prevent ME and seizure development. Interestingly, our data confirm a heterozygous phenotype in parents and siblings of individuals affected with KRD 14 with these individuals having a significantly larger head circumference (Z‐score 0.78; see Fig 1C ) than the general population, and anecdotal psychiatric manifestations.

We define isolated ketotic hypoglycemia as an important feature of KRD and recommend monitoring for hyperglycemia in infancy and childhood particularly during periods of intercurrent illness. We also identify other endocrinopathies as novel features of KRD, including precocious puberty and hypo/hyperthyroidism. Additional previously unrecognized features include skeletal abnormalities, ophthalmic manifestations, and recurrent infections.

As there are no published studies on human KRD neuropathology, the Kptn −/− mouse provides the only platform to assess the effects of Kptn loss on the developing brain. Brain imaging studies in KRD have shown brain enlargement in most individuals with subtle and infrequent abnormalities but no evidence for malformation of cortical development. In the Kptn−/− mouse, although there were no changes in laminar organization as evidenced by expression and distribution of layer markers CTIP2 and SATB, we identified numerous heterotopic neurons within the subcortical white matter suggesting an effect on neuronal migration due to loss of Kptn. In support of this finding, focal Kptn knockout via IUE also led to heterotopic neurons in the subcortical white matter. These observations were similar to those in Pretzel syndrome, 20 an ME syndrome linked to mutations in STRADA. The lamination of Strada KO mouse and human Pretzel syndrome cortex is intact but contains subcortical white matter heterotopic neurons and focal Strada KO via IUE resulted in heterotopic neurons in the subcortical white matter. 19 , 21 , 22 Heterotopic neurons have been linked to epilepsy, although neither seizures nor inter‐ictal abnormalities were detected in the Kptn−/− mice.

Both in vitro and in vivo experiments clearly demonstrate that Kptn loss leads to mTOR pathway activation that is reversible with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin. These data are similar to reports in SZT2‐ 23 , 24 and KICS2 ‐ 25 related disorders, where knockout in vitro leads to enhanced mTOR signaling, expanding the notion of a clinical subgroup of individuals with LoF variants in KICSTOR components (“KICSTORopathies”). Whereas sirolimus treatment did not lead to seizure reduction in 2 individuals, these 2 single patient trials do not define failure of mTOR inhibitors in KRD. Indeed, in the EXIST3 trial of everolimus in TSC, 17 60% of treated individuals did not show improved seizure control and approximately 10% showed exacerbation of their seizures. As both treated individuals were teenagers, it is very likely that earlier age intervention could have a beneficial effect. Indeed, brain overgrowth in KRD occurs postnatally in the first 6 months of life suggesting a potential early therapeutic window when treatment intervention may be beneficial. In view of the broad phenotypic spectrum we have defined, we submit that further preclinical work is necessary to more fully define the relationship between changes in mTOR signaling, seizures, and neurobehavioral features in KRD before a future larger clinical trial with mTORis is considered in KRD.
